summary: Barnard's Star is a small, cool red dwarf about 6 light-years away, and it moves across our sky faster than any other star. Comparing images from 2010 and 2026, WANDERERS measured it shifting 163 arcseconds, about 26.5 SPHEREx pixels. That works out to 10.39 arcseconds per year, matching the Gaia DR3 catalogue to within 0.1 percent, so we are highly confident. One caveat: all 173 SPHEREx measurements are flagged because the star is too bright for SPHEREx, so we have no reliable spectrum.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: Three checks agree. Between 2010 and 2026 the star moved 163 arcseconds, about 26.5 SPHEREx pixels. That works out to 10.39 arcseconds per year, which matches Gaia DR3's catalogue speed to within 0.1 percent. Gaia DR3 also lists this source. Its large parallax, about 0.547 arcseconds, means it is very close. Caveat: all 173 SPHEREx measurements are flagged as too bright, so there's no reliable spectrum.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: The weakest point is brightness. All 173 SPHEREx measurements are flagged because Barnard's Star is too bright for the detector, so there is no reliable SPHEREx spectrum. Overexposed images can also make the star's exact center harder to pin down. The east-west part of the measured motion differs from Gaia's by about 0.02 arcseconds per year, though the total speed matches. A bigger mismatch would make me less sure.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE photographed this patch of sky around 2010, and SPHEREx did in 2025 and 2026. Together they cover about 16 years. Over that time Barnard's Star moved 163 arcseconds, which is easy to measure. SPHEREx's own two visits are only about half a year apart, which is too short to pin down the speed well. Barnard's Star is too bright for SPHEREx, so all 173 of its measurements are flagged and we show no spectrum.
